title: Even one (Avot 3:6)
hook: ten who study together have the Presence among them, and so do five, three, two, even one
tomorrow: what do you give when nothing is really yours?

segments.voice: A week of chapter three: Akavia's three questions, the fish with no ruler, two on a couch, three at a table, the lonely hours, and yesterday's line: one yoke lightens others.
screen: `ONE YOKE LIGHTENS OTHERS.` → `A WEEK OF CHAPTER THREE.`

segments.voice: Rehearsal's canceled, the friend you study with is home sick, and it's just you, a mug going cold, and the page. Does that count, with nobody to argue with? Rabbi Chalafta ben Dosa counts down in Avot, and the answer is at the bottom of his list. Ten who sit and study, the Shechinah is among them. Five. Three. Two. And even one.
screen: `JUST YOU AND THE PAGE.` → `TEN, FIVE, THREE, TWO.` → `AND EVEN ONE.`

segments.voice: Each number gets its own verse. For ten, the psalm's "congregation", read as a minyan, the gathering of ten for prayer. For the last step, Exodus: "in all places where I record my name I will come unto thee, and I will bless thee." Thee: one person. Why count down at all, when the last step would cover everything? Some readers hear it as a ladder of encouragement: a hall full of voices, a few friends around a table, a pair on a couch, a commuter with a page on a train. Every rung keeps the same promise, and the list refuses to leave anyone off the bottom. So the countdown ends where the week began, with a single reader. Here's the week in one breath. Akavia said know whence, whither, before whom. Chanina said pray for order. Chananiah said the Presence rests between two. Shimon put a word on the table. Chanina ben Chakhinai warned that an empty heart, not the night, is the danger. Nechunia said one yoke lightens others. And now: even one.
screen: `TEN, A MINYAN.` · `THEE: ONE PERSON.` · `SIX SAYINGS, ONE WEEK.` · `EVEN ONE COUNTS.` · then, large: `EVEN ONE.`

segments.voice: Open one text you love, a page of Avot, a psalm, a poem, and read a single line slowly, alone. Then read it again out loud, quietly, with the room as your only audience. Let the words hang there for a moment before you close the book.
Even one: the bottom of Rabbi Chalafta's count, the solitary reader, and the Shechinah still comes.
Your line: even one. No minyan needed for a page and a quiet room. Next week, a new page.
